items.bodyEn: The shogunate allowed neither bridge nor ferry across the Ōi, so travelers were carried: on a porter's shoulders or on a litter borne by several men. Each morning the river office measured the depth and set the fare, from thigh-deep up to armpit-deep. Higher than that, the crossing closed and inns on both banks filled for days.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō 'Shimada: Ōigawa Sungan'; Shimada river-crossing site

items.bodyEn: An old packhorse driver's song sums up the road: Hakone's eight ri can be crossed even by horse, but the Ōi is a river you cannot cross for trying. Listen to the grammar: 馬でも 'even by horse' is the でも you meet at this station, and 越すに越されぬ sets the verb against its own negative.
items.ja: {箱根八里|はこねはちり}は{馬|うま}でも{越|こ}すが、{越|こ}すに{越|こ}されぬ{大井川|おおいがわ}
items.kana: はこねはちりはうまでもこすが、こすにこされぬおおいがわ
items.sourceNote: Hakone mago-uta, traditional packhorse-driver song (public domain)

items.titleEn: Hair, God, Paper: Three かみ
items.bodyEn: The shimada-mage, the classic bridal hairstyle, is said to take its name from this post town, so learn the word for hair. In Tokyo pitch, 髪 hair and 紙 paper are ka-MI, dropping on the particle: ka-MI-ga, が low. 神 god is KA-mi: high, then down, and が stays low. Hair and paper match; the god stands apart.

〜ても concedes a condition that may or may not happen: 雨が降っても行く, 'I'll go even if it rains'. 〜のに looks back at a fact that already holds and adds surprise or complaint: 雨なのに来た, 'you came even though it's raining'. Use ても for open possibilities, のに for settled facts, and keep のに out of requests and invitations; there it sounds reproachful.
items.ja: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っても{行|い}く。
